Hey! So I tried growing things in pots for a while and I'm not a total dumbass. Here's what I learned:

Tomatoes are a great starter plant, but they have a really difficult period. From seeds to seedlings, they're fragile as hell. If you start from seed, fully expect 14/15 of your plants to die off or just be useless little spindly abortions that never do anything useful.

PLANNING PHASE

Why did you choose Beefsteak? There are so many tomato varieties, you can buy entire seed catalogs dedicated to nothing but tomatoes. I'm not joking. https://www.totallytomato.com/

Before you go much further, you should decide what you want to do with your tomatoes. Do you want cherry tomatoes for a salad? Do you want something to slice up for BLTs? Do you want to process them down and make pasta sauce? Do you just want something cool to look at and fill your room with that delicious tomato-plant smell? There's no wrong answer - the only 'wrong' kind is the kind you don't end up eating.

There are Determinate and Indeterminate varieties of tomato. For a potted plant, you want Determinate. This means the plant has a 'determined' size they will grow to, then they'll stop growing and just use all their energy to make tomatoes. The Indeterminate variety will continue growing without limit - which means they'll quickly outstrip what sounds like a small windowsill or porch pot.

STARTING FROM SEEDS

So you need to start a shit ton of little baby tomatoes. (Peppers are the same, by the way.) Don't try and put them in the pot at first, that's just for the badass few that make it to the end. Start with a cardboard egg carton. Put a tablespoon of extremely loose soil in each egg slot, and drop 2-3 seeds in each hole. These are like Soviet foot soldiers, you expect at least one or two to die before anything useful gets done.

Protect your early seedlings from large swings in temperature and humidity. They will germinate with moisture and heat, but they can easily cook or freeze. Once they grow into long spindly seedlings they will be very sensitive to moisture and can easily dry out and die. Even if they don't die at first, letting a wounded seedling limp along is rarely going to do anything but waste your time before dying anyway. If they don't get a good start in life, they are usually garbage.

You can spend something like $30 for a covered plastic container, heater pad, and little compressed-fiber pucks that are designed to start seedlings in the best conditions possible. This is generally worth the investment if you want multiple plants, but for a single pot it might just be worth it to buy a healthy plant from a nursery somewhere. You're at about the break-even point. If you want to further invest in more gardening later I'd say invest in the little grow box. Otherwise, a single plant is only $5-10 at a nursery and is much more likely to live but will never be more than just the one plant.

I can't emphasize enough how loose the soil should be. Tomato roots are thin and flimsy. I would mix potting soil 50/50 with perlite, or even start the seeds in 100% perlite and water them with a soil tea. The point is that they can't send roots through heavy compact soil well, and need help getting started.

Once seedlings get started they'll be long and spindly. They'll fall all over each other, but as long as they stay moist you'll be okay. You can bury the spindly stems in more soil and they'll convert into root structure, which helps get the plant established. Just be careful - no matter how gentle you are, handling a young seedling like this causes damage.

SEEDLING TO PLANT STAGE

This is the toughest part. Up until now, the seedlings have been in perfect conditions. Humid, warm, protected, they should all have germinated and all be growing. Now's the time to harden them to real conditions and find out which are strong enough to survive.

This is called "hardening" and it's just training the plants through stress to build up their own tolerances to things like drought and wind. Just like people, they won't learn to handle adversity through any other means.

Move gradually and slowly expose the seedlings to more and more open air. Eventually you should have the top of the box open completely and they'll be getting 100% of their water from the soil. If they seem healthy enough, consider a fan or open window to stress the stems into tougher structures. Later on, the plants will become hardy enough to handle nights outside.

You should expect to lose plants through this process. You planted 20 of them, right? This is the way you'll find out which were the toughest. Once you have plants that are healthy enough to be transplanted, choose the best 1-3 and transplant them into the final pot.

Tomatoes do the most growing in the early morning, so water them around 5-7AM and they'll do best. They'll happily take as much sun as you have to give, but beware of the pot getting cooked in the heat. (Roots are far less tolerant to heat and dryness than leaves!)

Best of luck, and be sure to give us an update to how things are going!
